title: Atomic-Scale Imaging of Lattice Relaxation and Topological Flat Bands in Helical Trilayer Graphene
authors: Shudan Jiang, Zonglin Li, Yu Gu, Liang Liu, Dandan Guan, Yaoyi Li, Hao Zheng, Canhua Liu, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Shengwei Jiang, Xiaoxue Liu, Zhiwen Shi, Guorui Chen, Jinfeng Jia, Tingxin Li, Can Li, Shiyong Wang
abstract: Helical trilayer graphene (HTG) has emerged as a highly tunable moire quantum material that hosts strong electronic correlations and nontrivial band topology. However, the atomic-scale lattice structure and local electronic properties have remained largely unexplored. Here we present a comprehensive real-space study of HTG using a combination of scanning near-field optical microscopy and low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy. We directly image supermoire lattice relaxation, revealing large triangular domains separated by sharp domain walls, as well as stripe domains connected by smoothly varying boundaries. Atomic-scale spectroscopy uncovers flat bands with a honeycomb electronic texture and one-dimensional boundary states confined to domain walls. By systematically varying the twist angle, we identify a magic angle of approximately 1.9°, substantially larger than the 1.6 degree predicted by theory. Our results establish a direct microscopic link between lattice relaxation and flat bands in HTG.
summary: This paper provides a comprehensive real-space study of Helical Trilayer Graphene, using STM and SNOM to image supermoiré lattice relaxation. The authors successfully linked the observed lattice domain structure to the emergence of topological flat bands, identifying a magic angle of 1.9° through both structural and spectroscopic measurements.
main_problem: The study aims to bridge the gap between the atomic-scale lattice reconstruction and the electronic properties, specifically the topological flat bands, in Helical Trilayer Graphene (HTG).
main_result: The research established a direct microscopic link showing that lattice relaxation dictates the domain structure, which in turn hosts narrow, topologically nontrivial moiré bands. Furthermore, a magic angle of approximately 1.9° was identified.
method: The work combines experimental techniques like Scanning Near-Field Optical Microscopy (SNOM) and low-temperature Scanning Tunneling Microscopy/Spectroscopy (LT-STM/STS) with lattice-relaxation simulations.
model_or_system: The physical system is Helical Trilayer Graphene (HTG), a moire quantum material formed by twisting three graphene layers. The study investigates the supermoiré lattice relaxation, which creates large domains separated by sharp domain walls.
key_observables: Supermoiré lattice relaxation patterns (triangular/stripe domains), flat bands with honeycomb texture, one-dimensional boundary states, and the local Density of States (DOS) measured via STS.
important_parameters: Twist angle ($	heta$), strain, and carrier density (gate-tunable). A key finding is the magic angle of $\approx 1.9^\circ$.
main_assumptions: The study assumes that the electronic structure is governed by the underlying lattice relaxation and domain morphology, although it notes limitations in resolving correlated gaps at integer fillings.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device architecture and supermoiré reconstruction via AFM/SNOM, the honeycomb moiré lattice structure, and the dependence of the DOS on the twist angle, confirming the magic angle.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first visualizing the supermoiré reconstruction using microscopy, then using STS to map the electronic structure, confirming flat bands and boundary states, and finally correlating these electronic features with the lattice parameters to determine the magic angle.
why_interesting: The direct experimental mapping of structural relaxation to topological electronic features provides a concrete platform for studying correlated electron physics in tunable 2D materials, which is highly relevant to understanding emergent quantum states.

Figure 1b illustrates the helical twisted trilayer graphene structure and its reconstruction into a triangular supermoiré pattern. This reconstruction originates from the interference between the moiré lattices generated by the two twist angles, θ₁ and θ₂. For equal twist angles (θ₁ = θ₂ = θ), the moiré patterns of the upper and lower graphene bilayers are rotated relative to one another, producing a long-wavelength supermoiré structure [36,46]. The resulting hierarchy of length scales, from the atomic lattice to the moiré and supermoiré periods, strongly amplifies the effects of lattice relaxation.

Figure 2 | Topological flat bands and honeycomb electronic texture in HTG. (a) Schematic illustration of the atomic stacking configurations at the high-symmetry sites of a moiré unit cell. (b) STM topography resolving the emergent honeycomb moiré lattice. (c) Calculated band structure of HTG at a twist angle of 1.65°. (d) Experimental dI/dV spectra acquired at the representative sites marked in (b), together with the calculated density of states. (e) Gate-dependent dI/dV spectra measured as a function of graphite back-gate voltage, revealing the filling evolution of the narrow moiré bands.
